extracted.intended_audience: federal agency regulatory analysts, OIRA reviewers, and policy staff preparing regulatory impact analyses under OMB Circular A-4
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and reviewing federal regulatory impact analyses (RIAs) under OMB Circular A-4, including baseline selection, identification of needs for regulation, alternative approaches, and benefit-cost estimation methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline_should_reflect_relevant_final_or_reasonably_expected_rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytical baselines should attempt to reflect relevant final rules (especially if their requirements are being modified by the regulation under consideration) and proposed rules or other previously announced policy changes that the agency is reasonably certain will be finalized before the rule under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects of regulatory and other policy changes induced by the regulation under consideration should generally be attributed to the future actions themselves. Agencies may reflect likely future government programs/policies in either the primary or a supplemental baseline, and should carefully describe the ways those future programs/policies may affect the analysis. Consult OMB for case-specific guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do_not_attribute_effects_induced_by_federal_action_to_primary_baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: The effects of any future policies induced by the federal action under consideration should not be incorporated into the baseline for analysis of the federal action under consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preserves clarity about which impacts are due to the regulatory alternatives versus subsequent actions. If future government actors' behavior is relevant, include such effects only in a supplemental baseline and support predictions with reasonable evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline_must_be_analytically_reasonable_forecast
rubrics_metrics.description: A baseline should be 'an analytically reasonable forecast of the way the world would look absent the regulatory action being assessed, including any expected changes to current conditions over time.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should support predictions with reasonable evidence; do not simply assume the world will remain unchanged or that it will resemble the present without justification. Predictions should be justified and described transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre_statutory_vs_post_statutory_baselines (without-statute/with-statute)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an agency’s first regulatory action implementing a new statutory authority, agencies should generally assess effects against a pre-statutory (now termed 'without-statute') baseline; but if substantial portions merely restate statutory requirements that are self-implementing or the agency has essentially no regulatory discretion, a post-statutory ('with-statute') baseline may be used to focus on discretionary elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB expects agencies to use without-statute baselines in all cases except rare instances where the agency has essentially no discretion. If the agency lacks discretion but a without-statute baseline would be informative, agencies may still produce it; weigh benefits against analytic costs and consult OMB when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: When_to_use_without_statute_baselines_consider_burden_and_value
rubrics_metrics.description: Producing analyses using without-statute baselines can be burdensome, especially when the statute's effect is unclear but marginal effects of regulatory alternatives beyond the statute are clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should weigh the analytic costs versus the informational value to policymakers/public and may consult OMB on whether producing a without-statute baseline is worthwhile in cases with limited agency discretion. Examples (e.g., EPA HFC phasedown) can illustrate mixed statutory/directive and discretionary elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_of_multiple_baselines_when_appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should consider comparing regulatory effects against multiple baselines when informative (for example, a baseline that accounts for previously issued regulations and one that also accounts for sub-regulatory actions or interim final rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple baselines allow policymakers/public to consider marginal effects relative to binding rules and relative to non-binding guidance that could be rescinded. Include already-incurred compliance costs in baselines where relevant (e.g., when assessing a clarification, delay, revision, or reversal). Analysts are encouraged to update older analyses with newly available data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify_potential_needs_for_federal_regulatory_action_with_evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements about a need for federal regulatory action should generally be supported by evidence in the regulatory analysis; the process of identifying needs is iterative and the analysis can reveal that an assumed need is not present or may identify additional regulatory needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when implementing or interpreting statutory requirements, agencies should conduct reasonable inquiries to identify other needs for federal regulatory action. Use the analysis to test whether a need exists in the particular regulatory context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Model_market_failures_and_other_distortions_explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analyses should begin with modeling relevant distortions (market failures and other frictions) as a standard starting point for evaluating regulatory interventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expand consideration beyond simple externalities to include common pool resources, club goods, public goods, network benefits, and a more detailed discussion of market power sources and effects. Make clear the connection between identified distortions and the rationale for regulatory intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider_improving_government_operations_and_distributional_fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Improving government operations and service delivery, promoting distributional fairness and equity, and protecting civil rights and civil liberties or advancing democratic values can be appropriate potential needs for federal regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These considerations are not new to Circular A-4; Executive Orders direct that net benefits should include distributive impacts and equity and that agencies consider values difficult to quantify. Agencies should include these potential needs where relevant and support them with analysis/evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral_biases_as_potential_justification_require_high_quality_evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavioral biases may justify regulatory intervention and adjustments to valuation (e.g., using values not equal to observed willingness-to-pay or willingness-to-accept), but such uses require high-quality evidence that the bias is observed in or applicable to the specific regulatory context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental evidence alone, especially from non-consequential settings, is insufficient. Analysts should carefully consider whether observed behavior reflects rational preferences or behavioral bias and apply the same evidentiary standards used for other inputs to regulatory analysis. Document applicability to consequential settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account_for_biases_in_both_regulated_parties_and_regulators
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that both regulated parties and government regulators can exhibit behavioral biases, and if such biases in public institutions cause failures to maximize social welfare, they should be considered in analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If evidence shows regulatory institutions fail due to bias, this constitutes a failure of public institutions and should be addressed within Circular A-4 analytical framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider_costs_of_paternalism_and_individual_autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations that address behavioral biases may impose costs (e.g., to individual autonomy) that could be substantial and should be considered in regulatory analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such costs can be discussed as non-monetized costs where evidence exists. Agencies should include discussion of autonomy/paternalism costs when relevant to the choice of regulatory intervention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show_whether_federal_regulation_is_best_level_of_action
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses should consider whether federal regulation is the best way to solve the problem, including whether State, local, territorial, or Tribal regulation may be preferable for localized problems or as testing grounds for alternative policies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the learning value of deferring to States, regional preference differences, and the national costs of a fragmented regulatory system (e.g., increased compliance costs for firms). Agencies should analyze alternatives to federal action and weigh tradeoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare_alternative_regulatory_approaches_design_vs_performance
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating alternative regulatory approaches, consider design (specification) standards versus performance standards and the compliance implications of each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responding to comments, the final Circular clarifies compliance considerations and supplements language on methods to enhance compliance. Agencies should consider compliance costs and methods to promote compliance when choosing between approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_inefficient_distribution_of_fixed_regulatory_costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations should not inefficiently place heavier fixed-cost burdens on particular segments of an industry (e.g., smaller vs. larger firms) solely because one segment can better afford them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing disproportionate fixed costs on the most productive firms can be inefficient if costs exceed marginal harms caused. Consider distributional incidence of fixed costs and potential distortions in competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design_regulations_to_facilitate_data_collection_and_learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should design regulations and regulatory processes to facilitate data collection that can inform future evaluations of regulatory costs and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tools include pilot programs and learning-by-variation; agencies may adopt approaches that promote collection of relevant data for retrospective review and future analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Update_and_expand_methods_for_developing_benefit_and_cost_estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing benefit and cost estimates should incorporate updated material on revealed preference methods, stated preference methods, benefit-transfer methods, general equilibrium analysis, and accounting for non-monetized effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed revisions elaborate on earlier material with references to contemporary academic methods; OMB requested comment on generalizing guidance related to econometrics and applied statistics and collecting relevant content in one section.

rubrics_metrics.name: WTP_vs_WTA_use_professional_judgment_and_acknowledge_constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice between willingness-to-pay (WTP) and willingness-to-accept (WTA) measures should be guided by the available evidence; agencies should use professional judgment rather than a blanket preference for WTP or WTA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence availability may constrain choice; sometimes WTA estimates (e.g., VSL from wage compensation) are appropriate. Agencies may use one measure as a proxy for the other where justified, and should consider whether observed WTA-WTP differences are explicable by rational behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate_use_of_revealed_and_stated_preference_methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Revealed preference and stated preference methods should be used consistent with contemporary economic literature and with an understanding of their limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposed revisions provide a more balanced perspective on stated preference methods than the 2003 version; analysts should apply these methods appropriately and document limitations and assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply_and_document_benefit_transfer_methods_carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefit-transfer methods should be applied using updated guidance and documented to ensure credibility of transferred estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several commenters supported updated material on benefit-transfer methods; agencies should follow best practices in transferring valuations across contexts and be transparent about uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish_additional_benefits_and_costs_from_main_purpose_impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analyses should include significant consequences (direct/indirect, intended/unintended) but clearly distinguish additional benefits or costs from impacts related to the main purpose of the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear distinction supports transparency and helps decisionmakers and the public understand which effects are central to the regulation’s purpose versus ancillary effects; non-monetized additional effects should be noted and explained.
